passages.title: Should Schools Ban Smartphones?
text: In recent years, a growing number of countries, including the Netherlands and Brazil, have restricted the use of smartphones in schools. Supporters claim that phones distract students and harm their learning, while opponents argue that phones can be valuable learning tools. The question of whether schools should ban smartphones remains hotly debated.

Those who support a ban argue that smartphones divide students' attention. Notifications from social media and messaging apps interrupt concentration, and even a silent phone on the desk can tempt students to check it. Some studies have found that students in schools with phone restrictions performed slightly better in exams, particularly lower-achieving students. Supporters also believe that a ban encourages face-to-face interaction during breaks and reduces cyberbullying during school hours.

Opponents, however, point out that smartphones give students instant access to dictionaries, calculators, educational videos, and online research tools. In schools with limited computers, a phone may be the only digital device a student can use. Many parents also want their children to carry phones for safety reasons, so that they can be contacted in an emergency. Furthermore, opponents argue that schools should teach students to manage technology responsibly rather than simply removing it, since students will have to control their own phone use at university and at work.

Between these two positions, many schools have adopted partial approaches. Some require phones to be kept in lockers during lessons but allow them during breaks; others allow phones only when a teacher asks students to use them for a specific task.
In the end, the most effective policy may depend on each school's situation. What matters is that rules are clear, consistently applied, and focused on helping students learn.

passages.title: Vertical Farming: Food for Growing Cities
text: By 2050, around two-thirds of the world's population is expected to live in cities. Feeding these urban populations while protecting forests and farmland is one of the great challenges of this century. Vertical farming, the practice of growing crops in stacked layers inside buildings, offers a promising solution, and cities should actively support its development.

The main advantage of vertical farming is efficiency. Because crops are grown in layers, a vertical farm can produce many times more food per square metre than a conventional field. Most vertical farms use hydroponic systems, in which plants grow in nutrient-rich water instead of soil, recycling water so efficiently that they use up to ninety percent less than traditional farming.

Vertical farms also protect harvests from the weather. Inside a controlled environment, crops are not affected by droughts, floods, or pests, so they can be harvested all year round without chemical pesticides. As climate change makes weather patterns less predictable, this reliability becomes increasingly valuable.

In addition, growing food inside cities shortens supply chains. Vegetables that once travelled hundreds of kilometres by truck can be harvested and sold on the same day, reducing transport costs, fuel use, and food loss.

Critics correctly note that vertical farms require a great deal of electricity for lighting and climate control, which makes their produce expensive, and that they are currently suitable mainly for leafy greens and herbs rather than staple crops like rice. However, LED lights are becoming more efficient, and farms powered by renewable energy can greatly reduce their environmental impact. With the right support, vertical farming can become an important part of how cities feed themselves.

passages.title: Learning from the 2018 Palu Disaster
text: On 28 September 2018, a magnitude 7.5 earthquake struck Central Sulawesi. Within minutes, a tsunami hit the coast of Palu Bay, and in several neighbourhoods the ground itself turned into a flowing mud in a process called liquefaction. More than 4,000 people died or were reported missing.

Experts who studied the disaster identified several lessons. First, the tsunami arrived very quickly, in some places within only a few minutes of the shaking. This meant that there was little time for official warnings to reach people. Residents who knew that strong shaking near the coast is itself a natural warning and moved immediately to higher ground were more likely to survive.

Second, the communication system failed at a critical time. Power cuts and damaged telecommunications towers prevented many warning messages from being received. The sirens that were supposed to warn coastal communities were, in several places, not working.

Third, liquefaction caused enormous damage in areas that had not been considered dangerous. Houses in the neighbourhoods of Petobo and Balaroa were carried away or swallowed as the soil lost its strength. Afterwards, the government declared some of these areas unsafe for rebuilding and relocated residents.

These lessons suggest that technology alone cannot protect communities. Warning systems must be maintained, but people also need to understand natural warning signs, know their evacuation routes, and live in areas whose risks have been properly mapped. Disaster education, therefore, should be a regular part of school life in every region at risk.

passages.title: Fast Fashion: Who Pays the Price?
text: Clothes have never been cheaper. Fast-fashion brands release new collections every few weeks, and a T-shirt can cost less than a meal. Many people see this as a benefit, but it is time we recognized the hidden costs of fast fashion and changed the way we buy clothes.

The environmental cost is enormous. The fashion industry is a major user of water: producing a single cotton T-shirt can require more than two thousand litres. Dyeing and treating fabrics pollutes rivers in many producing countries, and synthetic fabrics such as polyester are made from oil and shed microplastic fibres when washed. Because cheap clothes are designed to be worn only a few times, huge quantities end up in landfills each year.

There is also a human cost. To keep prices low, many factories pay workers very low wages and require long working hours. In 2013, the collapse of the Rana Plaza garment factory building in Bangladesh killed more than 1,100 workers and drew global attention to unsafe working conditions in the industry.

Consumers have the power to change this. We can buy fewer but better-quality clothes, repair items instead of throwing them away, and choose second-hand clothing. Before buying, we should ask ourselves whether we really need the item and how many times we will wear it. We can also support brands that are open about where and how their clothes are made.
Fashion can be fun and creative without harming the planet or the people who make our clothes. The cheapest T-shirt is often the most expensive one for the world.

passages.title: Digital Payments for Small Traders
text:
Text A (a summary of a central bank report)
Since its launch in 2019, the national QR code payment standard, QRIS, has been adopted by tens of millions of merchants in Indonesia, the large majority of them micro and small businesses. A single QR code allows customers to pay using many different banking and e-wallet apps. The report states that digital payments help small traders record transactions automatically, reduce the risk of receiving counterfeit money, and build a financial history that can make it easier to obtain loans.

Text B (from an interview with a street-food seller in Surabaya)
"I started using the QR code two years ago because many young customers didn't carry cash. It's practical, and I don't have to look for small change. But not everything is perfect. Sometimes the internet signal is weak and payments take a long time to confirm, so a queue forms. A few times, customers showed me fake payment screenshots, and I only realized later that the money never arrived. Now I always wait for the notification sound before handing over the food. Most of my older customers still pay with cash, so I need both."
